Series::erf¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::erf() const -> Series
Series& Series::erf_()

What It Does¶

Applies the Gauss error function elementwise.

For a scalar input x, the error function is the area under a bell curve, scaled so that it approaches 1:

erf(x) = (2 / sqrt(pi)) * integral from 0 to x of exp(-t^2) dt

That integral has no elementary closed form, so erf() is a primitive: the library evaluates it directly rather than composing it from exp, log, and friends.

A few properties fall straight out of the definition and are worth carrying in your head:

  • erf(0) = 0, because the integral over an empty interval is zero.

  • erf(-x) = -erf(x). The integrand exp(-t^2) is symmetric about t = 0, so the signed area is an odd function.

  • erf(x) is bounded. As x -> +inf it approaches +1; as x -> -inf it approaches -1. The 2 / sqrt(pi) factor is exactly what makes those limits land on +/-1 rather than on +/-sqrt(pi)/2.

  • erf is strictly increasing, because its integrand is strictly positive everywhere.

The single most common reason to reach for erf() is its link to the normal distribution. The cumulative distribution function of a standard normal is

Phi(x) = 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / sqrt(2)))

so anything phrased in terms of “probability a Gaussian draw falls below a threshold” is an erf() call in disguise. The Gaussian-error-linear-unit activation is built the same way.

erf() is an out-of-place unary transform: shape, dtype, and platform are preserved, no broadcasting is involved, and the result is a fresh Series. erf_() is the in-place spelling that overwrites the current storage.

Parameters¶

None.

The transform is fully determined by the input values.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self, each element replaced by erf(x). The out-of-place overload returns a new value; erf_() returns a reference to the mutated current series.

The result dtype matches the input dtype for the supported floating-point types. A float32 input produces a float32 result; a float64 input produces a float64 result.

Gradient¶

erf() is differentiable, and its backward rule is the derivative of the defining integral. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, differentiating the integral just evaluates the integrand at the upper limit:

d/dx erf(x) = (2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-x^2)

The constant 2 / sqrt(pi) is 1.1283791670955126. So the local multiplier is largest at x = 0, where it equals that constant exactly, and decays like a Gaussian as |x| grows. Far out in either tail the sensitivity is effectively zero, which mirrors the fact that erf() has flattened against +/-1 and is no longer responding to its input.

Because the backward multiplier is itself exp(-x^2) times a constant, it is smooth and composes cleanly through the chain rule with any surrounding computation.

Examples¶

The examples build up from the basic shape to dtype handling, the autograd rule, and the failure mode.

Example 1. The signed, bounded, odd shape on a symmetric grid of inputs.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0}).erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.9953, -0.8427, -0.5205, 0.0000, 0.5205, 0.8427, 0.9953]

The output is antisymmetric around the middle entry, and the middle entry is exactly 0.

Example 2. Saturation. Once |x| is past roughly 4, the result is +/-1 to the precision shown.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-4.0, -3.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0}).erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000, -1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000]

This is not an overflow. erf is bounded, so large-magnitude inputs simply map to the horizontal asymptotes.

Example 3. The transform is elementwise and shape-preserving on matrices.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {0.0, 0.5},
    {1.0, 2.0},
}).erf();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0.52049988],
  [0.84270079, 0.99532227]]

Example 4. A non-contiguous input is accepted. The result is a fresh contiguous series carrying the transformed values in the view’s visible order.

auto rows = pluss::make_series({
    {-1.0, 0.0, 1.0},
    {2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
});

std::cout << rows.transpose(0, 1).erf();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-0.84270079, 0.99532227],
  [0, 0.99997791],
  [0.84270079, 0.99999998]]

Example 5. float32 in, float32 out. erf() does not silently widen to float64.

auto f = pluss::make_series({-1.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, f.erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8427, 0.0000, 0.8427]

Example 6. Non-finite inputs follow the limits. NaN propagates, and the infinities map to the asymptotes.

double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({nan, inf, -inf}).erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, 1.0000, -1.0000]

Example 7. The backward multiplier is (2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-x^2). Here the reverse-mode sensitivity is compared against that formula evaluated by hand.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.erf();
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

auto manual = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
std::cout << "by formula=" << manual.mul(manual).neg().exp().mul(1.1283791670955126);

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.84270079, 0, 0.52049988, 0.84270079]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.4151075, 1.1283792, 0.87878258, 0.4151075]
by formula=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.4151075, 1.1283792, 0.87878258, 0.4151075]

The sensitivity peaks at x = 0 with value 1.1283792, which is 2 / sqrt(pi), and it is already symmetric because the derivative depends only on x^2.

Example 8. The rule composes. For erf(2x) the chain rule multiplies the local derivative by the inner slope 2:

d/dx erf(2x) = 2 * (2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-(2x)^2)

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.mul(2.0).erf();
y.sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.2568, 0.8302, 0.0413]

At x = 0 the value is 2 * 1.1283792 = 2.2568. By x = 1 the inner argument is 2, exp(-4) is tiny, and the sensitivity has nearly vanished.

Example 9. erf() is floating-point only. An integer or boolean input does not promote; it raises.

try {
  pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}).erf());
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

erf: dtype not implemented (float-only)

Convert first when the source column is integral:

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64).erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.8427, 0.9953]

Example 10. erf_() overwrites the current storage in place.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0});
a.erf_();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.8427, 0.9953]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • erf() requires a floating-point input. Integer and boolean series raise erf: dtype not implemented (float-only); call to() first.

  • The result is bounded in (-1, 1). Large-magnitude inputs are not an error and do not overflow; they saturate against +/-1.

  • Because the backward multiplier decays like exp(-x^2), gradients through erf() are effectively zero once |x| is large. A saturated erf() stops passing useful sensitivity to its input.

  • erf() is not erfc(). For tail probabilities where erf(x) is within rounding distance of 1, compute erfc(x) directly instead of 1 - erf(x).

  • NaN propagates unchanged.

Summary¶

erf() is the Gauss error function as a shape-preserving unary transform:

  • odd, strictly increasing, bounded in (-1, 1)

  • the bridge between raw inputs and standard-normal probabilities

  • differentiable with backward multiplier (2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-x^2)

  • floating-point only; convert integral inputs with to()

  • erf_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::erfc: the complementary error function 1 - erf(x), accurate in the tail where erf(x) rounds to 1.

  • Series::exp: the primitive that the backward rule of erf() is built from.

  • Series::sigmoid: another bounded, saturating, differentiable activation-style transform.
